s704_PP_r2:
Hello! Sure. Quick rule: we use a before a consonant sound (a pen) and an before a vowel sound (an apple).

Here is your first one. Write a or an: She has ___ orange in her bag.

Answer with only the missing word.
s710_PP_r2:
Hi! Good choice. We use the when we talk about the same thing again. Example: I have a dog. The dog is brown.

Try this. Write a or the: We have a garden. ___ garden is small.
s716_PP_r2:
Hello! Let's practise the. The first time we talk about a thing, we use a or an. When we talk about it again, we use the, because now we both know which one. Example: She has a cat. The cat is black.

Your turn. Write a or the: We have a garden. ___ garden is small.
s722_PP_r2:
Hello! Sure. Remember: can + base verb. No -s and no to after can. Example: He can cook. I can't sing.

Here is an exercise. Correct this sentence: 'She can swims.'
s728_PP_r2:
Hello! Yes. Two rules: start every sentence with a capital letter, and end it with a full stop (.).

Rewrite this sentence correctly: my brother likes tea
s734_PP_r2:
Hi! Great topic. Remember: every sentence starts with a capital letter and ends with a full stop. Also, the word I is always a capital letter, in any place in the sentence.

Rewrite this sentence correctly: i am ten years old
s740_PP_r2:
Hello! Sure. Remember: I am, he/she/it is, you/we/they are. In English we cannot leave this word out. We say She is a teacher, not She a teacher.

First one. Write am, is or are: I ___ a student. (Answer with only the missing word.)
s746_PP_r2:
Hello! Here is the rule: at + clock time (at 7 o'clock), on + day (on Monday), in + month (in July).

Try this. Write in, on or at: My train leaves ___ 5 o'clock.
s752_PP_r2:
Hi! Quick reminder: we use at for clock times, on for days, and in for months. For example: at 7 o'clock, on Monday, in July.

Your first exercise. Write in, on or at: They get married ___ April.
s758_PP_r2:
Hello! Sure. Use there is with one thing: There is a table. Use there are with two or more things: There are two chairs.

Complete this sentence: '___ three windows in my room.'
s764_PP_r2:
Hello! In English the order is: subject + verb + object. Example: Sam plays football. Time or place goes at the end: Sam plays football on Fridays.

Put these words in order: plays / Sam / chess / on Mondays
s770_PP_r2:
Hi! Remember: subject first, then the verb, then the object. Words like always, usually and often go before the main verb. Example: My brother often reads books.

Put these words in order: usually / we / lunch / have
s776_PP_r2:
Hello! Sure, let's practise classroom words: desk, chair, pen, book, board, bag. We can say: This is a pen.

Complete this sentence: 'I sit on a ___.'
s782_PP_r2:
Hello! Good idea. With days and months we use small words before them: on + day (on Monday) and in + month (in July). With clock times we use at (at 7 o'clock).

Try this one. Write in, on or at: They get married ___ April.
s788_PP_r2:
Hi! Let's practise days and months with in, on and at. The rule: on for a day (on Monday), in for a month (in July), at for a clock time (at 5 o'clock).

Here is a sentence for you. Write in, on or at: My holiday is ___ August.
s794_PP_r2:
Hello! Sure. We introduce a family member with This is my ... Then we use he for a man or a boy, and she for a woman or a girl. Example: This is my sister. She is ten.

Complete: 'This is my brother. ___ is twelve.'
s800_PP_r2:
Hello! Let's practise food and drink words: bread, rice, apple, milk, egg, fish. We eat bread. We drink water.

What is the word? You drink it. It is white. ___
s806_PP_r2:
Hi! Sure. Here are some food words: bread, rice, apple, milk, egg, fish. We can say what we like: I like rice.

Complete: 'I eat an ___ every morning.' (It is a red or green fruit.)
s812_PP_r2:
Hello! Sure. Here are the places in a home: kitchen, bedroom, bathroom, garden. We say in the + place. Example: There is a tree in the garden.

Complete: 'I make toast in the ___.'
s818_PP_r2:
Hello! Let's practise time words. Sometimes people change the time in a dialogue, so look for the last time they say.

Read this:
A: Is the lesson at nine?
B: No, at ten.

What time is the lesson?
s824_PP_r2:
Hi! Sure. Quick help: quarter past = 15 minutes after the hour, half past = 30 minutes after, quarter to = 15 minutes before the hour. In a dialogue the time can change, so look for the final time.

A: Let's meet at half past four.
B: Sorry, I can't. Can we meet at quarter to six?
A: OK, no problem.

What time do they meet? Write it as a clock time.
s830_PP_r2:
Hello! Sure. In English, 'Give me ...' can sound rude. It is more polite to say Can I have ..., please? or I would like ..., please.

Make this polite: 'Give me a coffee.'
s836_PP_r2:
Hello! Sure. Short adjectives add -er: fast becomes faster. Some short adjectives also double the last letter: hot becomes hotter. Long adjectives use more: more beautiful. Then we use than. Example: A car is faster than a bike.

Complete: 'Cairo is ___ (big) than Luxor.'
s842_PP_r2:
Hi! Remember: short adjectives add -er (cheap, cheaper). Long adjectives use more + adjective (more beautiful). After that, use than.

Complete: 'This phone is ___ (expensive) than that one.'
s848_PP_r2:
Hello! Sure. We use and to add an idea, but to show a contrast, and because to give a reason. Example: She is happy because it is Friday.

Join these two sentences with but: 'The bus is cheap. It is slow.'
s854_PP_r2:
Hello! Sure. Always, usually, sometimes and never go before the main verb. Example: My brother usually gets up at seven. And remember: with he, she and it, the verb takes -s.

Put these words in order: always / she / breakfast / has
s860_PP_r2:
Hi! Good topic. always = every time, usually = most of the time, sometimes = some of the time, never = not at any time. They go before the main verb: I never have coffee in the evening.

Add usually to this sentence in the right place: 'My dad watches TV after dinner.'
s866_PP_r2:
Hello! Sure. For plans we use am/is/are + going to + verb. Example: I'm going to visit my aunt tomorrow.

Correct this sentence: 'I going to study tonight.'
s872_PP_r2:
Hello! Sure. Use many with things we can count (eggs, bottles). Use much with things we cannot count (rice, water).

Write much or many: How ___ bottles are there?
s878_PP_r2:
Hi! Quick rule: many + things we can count (many eggs), much + things we cannot count (much rice). We often use them in questions and in negative sentences.

Write much or many: How ___ milk is in the fridge?
s884_PP_r2:
Hello! Sure. To ask about the past, use Did + subject + base verb. Example: Did you go to the beach? (not 'Did you went'). With a question word: What did you do last weekend?

Make a question with did from these words: you / watch / a film / yesterday
s890_PP_r2:
Hello! Sure. Some verbs do not take -ed in the past. They change: go becomes went, buy becomes bought, see becomes saw.

Write the past form of 'have': Yesterday I ___ a big lunch.
s896_PP_r2:
Hi! Remember: irregular verbs change their form and do not take -ed. Example: I went to the market yesterday (not 'goed').

Write the past form of 'tell': Last night he ___ me a story.
s902_PP_r2:
Hello! Sure. For regular verbs, we add -ed to talk about finished actions in the past: play becomes played, visit becomes visited.

Complete with the past form of 'watch': Last weekend I ___ a football match on TV.
s908_PP_r2:
Hello! Sure. We use am/is/are + verb-ing for actions happening now. Example: Two children are playing football.

Imagine a park. Write one sentence about what a man is doing now. Use is + -ing.
s914_PP_r2:
Hi! Remember: I am + -ing, he/she/it is + -ing, you/we/they are + -ing. Don't forget am, is or are! Example: A woman is sitting under a tree.

Imagine a park now. Write two sentences about what people are doing.
s920_PP_r2:
Hello! Good question. We use some in positive sentences and polite requests: I'd like some water. We use any in most questions and in negative sentences: We don't have any rice.

Complete with some or any: 'Do you have ___ sandwiches?'
s926_PP_r2:
Hello! Sure. After he, she and it, we add -s to the verb in the present simple: I work, she works.

Here is your first one. Write the correct form: My sister ___ (play) tennis on Sundays. (Answer with only the verb.)
s932_PP_r2:
Hi! Remember: he/she/it + verb + -s. If the verb ends in -sh, -ch, -s, -x or -o, add -es: teach becomes teaches.

Write the correct form: He ___ (drink) tea in the morning. (Answer with only the verb.)
s938_PP_r2:
Hello! Sure. For hair and eyes, we use has: My aunt has long black hair. For height and personality, we use is: He is tall.

Complete: 'My cousin ___ brown eyes.' (has / have)
s944_PP_r2:
Hello! Sure. To ask the price, say How much is ...? for one thing and How much are ...? for more than one. To ask for a size or colour, say Do you have this in ...?

Correct this question: 'How much cost this hat?'
s950_PP_r2:
Hi! Let's practise shopping questions. Example: Do you have this shirt in blue? / How much are the socks?

You like a jacket, but you want it in small. What do you ask the shop assistant? Write a full question.
s956_PP_r2:
Hello! Sure. We say where people work with works in or works at. Example: A teacher works at a school.

Complete: 'A chef works in a ___.'
s962_PP_r2:
Hello! Sure. For the weather, we say It is + adjective: It is sunny today. Words: sunny, rainy, windy, cloudy, hot, cold.

Complete: 'Take an umbrella. It is ___ today.'
s968_PP_r2:
Hi! Remember, in English we always say It is ... for the weather: It is cold today (not 'Is cold').

Complete: 'My hat flew away! It is very ___.'
s980_PP_r2:
Hello! Of course. A quick refresher: the choice depends on the first sound, not the first letter, so we say an hour but a university.

First one. Write a or an: He wants ___ umbrella. (Answer with only the missing word.)
s986_PP_r2:
Hello! Happy to. A quick reminder: one-syllable adjectives usually take -er, longer adjectives take more, and a few are irregular, like good and better. Than introduces the second thing in the comparison.

Let's start. Complete: 'This phone is ___ (expensive) than that one.'
